parts.name: Part 1: Percentage basics

read.book: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude
read.where: Chapter 'Percentage': theory and solved examples (skip the exercises today)
read.why: Standard textbook, solved examples in the first half of the chapter

read.book: Kiran, SSC Maths Chapterwise Solved Papers
read.where: Chapter 'Percentage': read the first 10 solved questions to see the SSC style

notes: Percent means 'out of 100'. x% of y = (x/100) × y, and x% of y = y% of x (so 8% of 50 = 50% of 8 = 4).
Percentage change = (New − Old) / Old × 100.
If A is r% more than B, then B is r/(100+r) × 100 % less than A. If A is r% less than B, B is r/(100−r) × 100 % more than A. (20% more becomes 16.67% less.)
If price rises r%, to keep spending the same, consumption must fall by r/(100+r) × 100 %.
A number going from N to N×(100+r)/100 uses the multiplier method: 20% increase = ×1.2, 25% decrease = ×0.75.

examples.q: What is 35% of 240?
28 is what percent of 80?
A number increased by 20% becomes 150. Find the number.
Price of sugar rises by 25%. By what percent must a family cut consumption to keep spending the same?
A's salary is 20% more than B's. By what percent is B's salary less than A's?

solve.label: Book practice, 60 minutes max
solve.book: RSA 'Percentage': solve the first 40 questions of the first exercise, in order. Tick the ones you got wrong.

solve.label: Previous-year questions
solve.book: KM 'Percentage': solve 25 questions, 45 seconds each. Skip any you cannot start in 10 seconds and come back.

parts.name: Part 2: Successive change and applications

read.book: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude
read.where: Same chapter 'Percentage': sections on population, successive changes, election and marks problems

read.book: Kiran, SSC Maths Chapterwise Solved Papers

notes: Two successive changes of a% and b%: net change = a + b + ab/100 (use negative for decrease). +10% then +20% = 10 + 20 + 2 = 32%.
+10% then −10% = 10 − 10 − 1 = −1%. A rise and equal fall is always a net loss.
Population: after n years at r% growth, P × (1 + r/100)^n. Use the multiplier: 10% growth twice = × 1.1 × 1.1 = × 1.21.
Marks and election problems: write what each % difference is worth in actual numbers, then scale up to 100%.
Shortcut: for 'fails by x marks' and 'passes with y extra marks', pass marks = obtained + x = obtained' − y. The difference in percentages equals x + y marks.

examples.q: Two successive increases of 10% and 20% equal what single increase?
A town of 20,000 grows 10% then falls 10%. Find the final population.
A candidate scores 35% and fails by 40 marks. Another scores 45% and gets 20 marks more than needed. Find the maximum marks and pass marks.
In a two-candidate election the winner gets 58% of votes and wins by 1,600. How many votes were cast?

solve.label: Book practice, 60 minutes max
solve.book: RSA 'Percentage': solve questions 41 to 80 of the first exercise, then the first 20 of the next exercise.

solve.label: Previous-year questions
solve.book: KM 'Percentage': solve 20 more questions. Write down one shortcut you learned.

parts.name: Part 3: Ratio, proportion and average

read.book: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude
read.where: Chapters 'Ratio & Proportion' and 'Average': theory and solved examples

read.book: Kiran, SSC Maths Chapterwise Solved Papers
read.where: Chapters 'Ratio and Proportion' and 'Average': first 10 solved questions each

notes: Ratio a:b = a/b. To split an amount in ratio a:b:c, one part = Amount / (a+b+c).
Compound ratio: multiply. To join A:B = 3:4 and B:C = 6:7, make B equal: A:B:C = 9:12:14 (multiply first by 3, second by 2).
Average = Sum / Count. If a number is added or removed, new sum = old sum ± that number, then divide by the new count.
Average of n consecutive numbers (or an AP) = middle value = (first + last) / 2.
If every term changes by x, the average changes by x. If every term is multiplied by x, the average is multiplied by x.
Ratio of ages: write ages as multiples (3x, 5x), then use the given sum or difference.

examples.q: Divide ₹4,200 in the ratio 2 : 3 : 7.
A : B = 3 : 4 and B : C = 6 : 7. Find A : B : C.
examples.s: Multiply A:B by 3 → 9:12, and B:C by 2 → 12:14.

examples.q: The average of 5 numbers is 27. If one number is removed the average of the rest is 25. Find the number removed.
The average age of 30 students is 14. With the teacher the average becomes 15. Find the teacher's age.
Two numbers are in the ratio 5 : 7 and their sum is 96. Find them.

solve.label: Book practice, 75 minutes max
solve.book: RSA 'Ratio & Proportion': first 30 questions. RSA 'Average': first 30 questions.

solve.label: Previous-year questions
solve.book: KM 'Ratio and Proportion': 15 questions. KM 'Average': 15 questions.

r.title: Reasoning: Number series, analogy, odd one out

parts.name: Part 1: Number series

read.book: R.S. Aggarwal, Verbal & Non-Verbal Reasoning
Kiran, SSC Reasoning Chapterwise Solved Papers

notes: Check in this order: (1) constant difference (AP), (2) constant ratio (GP), (3) differences that grow (+2, +4, +8 or +1, +2, +3), (4) squares or cubes (n² ± k, n³ ± k), (5) two interleaved series (odd and even positions), (6) primes, (7) multiply and add (×2 + 1).
Learn squares to 30 and cubes to 15. Most SSC series are built on them.
Write the differences under the series first. 70% of questions are solved by that single step.
If two numbers seem to jump randomly, test alternate terms separately.

solve.label: Book practice, 30 minutes
solve.book: RV 'Series Completion': first 30 number-series questions.

solve.label: Previous-year questions
solve.book: KR 'Number Series': 20 questions, 40 seconds each.

parts.name: Part 2: Analogy

read.book: R.S. Aggarwal, Verbal & Non-Verbal Reasoning
read.where: Chapter 'Analogy': number, letter and word analogies

read.book: Kiran, SSC Reasoning Chapterwise Solved Papers

notes: Find the relationship in the first pair, then apply it to the second pair. Say the relation in a sentence first.
Common word relations: worker to workplace, tool to function, part to whole, animal to young one or home, cause to effect, product to raw material.
Number analogies: square, cube, multiply, add, or a mix (a : a² + 1).
Letter analogies: write the alphabet positions (A=1 ... Z=26) and look at the shifts. Opposite letter of position n is 27 − n.

examples.s: The second is the square of the first.

examples.q: CAT : ECV :: DOG : ?
examples.s: Each letter moves +2: D→F, O→Q, G→I.

examples.q: Doctor : Hospital :: Teacher : ?
Pen : Write :: Knife : ?

solve.book: RV 'Analogy': 30 questions covering number, letter and word types.

solve.label: Previous-year questions
solve.book: KR 'Analogy': 20 questions.

parts.name: Part 3: Odd one out (classification)

read.book: R.S. Aggarwal, Verbal & Non-Verbal Reasoning
Kiran, SSC Reasoning Chapterwise Solved Papers

notes: Find the one property that three items share and one lacks. For numbers: prime, square, cube, multiple of k, odd or even, digit sum.
For letters: positions, vowels or consonants, skip pattern, reverse order.
For words: category (fruit, vegetable, bird, mammal), function, or a spelling pattern. Test two different rules before choosing.

examples.q: Mango, Apple, Potato, Banana
examples.s: A vegetable, the rest are fruits.

solve.label: Book practice, 30 minutes
solve.book: RV 'Classification': 30 questions.

solve.label: Previous-year questions
solve.book: KR 'Classification': 20 questions.

e.title: English: Parts of speech, tenses, subject-verb agreement

parts.name: Part 1: Parts of speech

read.book: Wren & Martin, High School English Grammar & Composition
read.where: Chapters on Noun, Pronoun, Adjective, Verb, Adverb, Preposition and Conjunction (read the rules, skip long exercises)

read.book: S.P. Bakshi, Objective General English
read.where: Chapter 'Parts of Speech' / 'Spotting Errors' sections on nouns, adjectives, adverbs

notes: Noun types: proper (Delhi), common (city), collective (team), abstract (honesty), material (gold).
Adjective describes a noun (tall boy). Adverb describes a verb, adjective or adverb (runs fast, very tall). Many words do both: hard, fast, early.
Good is an adjective; well is usually an adverb (He plays well). 'Well' is an adjective only for health (I am well).
A collective noun taken as one unit takes 'its': The committee has announced its decision.
Preposition links a noun to the rest of the sentence: on, in, at, by, for, with, of, to. Learn fixed pairs: good at, afraid of, senior to, prefer X to Y.
Conjunctions join: and, but, or, because, although, unless.

examples.q: 'She sings beautifully.' What is 'beautifully'?
'Honesty is the best policy.' What is 'Honesty'?
'He works hard.' What is 'hard'?
examples.s: It says how he works. In 'a hard task' it is an adjective.

examples.q: Fill: 'The committee has announced ___ decision.'

solve.label: Book practice, 45 minutes
solve.book: WM: do the short exercises on adjectives, adverbs and prepositions (about 40 sentences).

parts.name: Part 2: Tenses

read.book: Wren & Martin, High School English Grammar & Composition
read.where: Chapter 'The Verb: Tenses' and 'Sequence of Tenses'

read.book: S.P. Bakshi, Objective General English

notes: 12 tenses = 4 times (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous) × 3 (present, past, future).
Simple past goes with finished time: yesterday, last year, in 2010, ago.
Present perfect (has/have + V3) goes with: since, for, already, yet, just, ever, never. Since + point in time; for + period of time.
Past perfect (had + V3) is the earlier of two past actions: The train had left before we reached.
Future perfect (will have + V3) goes with 'by + future time'.
Conditionals: 1st: If + present, will. 2nd: If + past (were), would. 3rd: If + had + V3, would have + V3.
'No sooner had ... than' and 'Hardly had ... when' both take past perfect, with inversion.

examples.q: He ___ here since 2010. (live)
examples.s: 'Since' + point in time → present perfect continuous.

examples.q: The train ___ before we reached. (leave)
If I were you, I ___ accept it.
Hardly had I reached the station ___ the train left.

solve.label: Book practice, 45 minutes
solve.book: WM: tense exercises on present perfect, past perfect and sequence of tenses (about 40 sentences).

parts.name: Part 3: Subject-verb agreement

read.book: Wren & Martin, High School English Grammar & Composition
read.where: Chapter 'Concord' (Agreement of the verb with its subject)

read.book: S.P. Bakshi, Objective General English

notes: Each, every, either, neither, one of, anyone, everyone take a singular verb. 'One of the boys is'.
'The number of' is singular. 'A number of' is plural.
With 'along with', 'as well as', 'together with', 'with': the verb agrees with the FIRST subject.
With 'either ... or' and 'neither ... nor': the verb agrees with the NEARER subject.
Singular in form: news, mathematics, physics, economics, measles, furniture, advice, information, scenery.
Plural only: scissors, trousers, spectacles, people, police, cattle.
Two nouns for one person or idea take a singular verb: Bread and butter is my breakfast.

examples.q: One of my friends ___ coming today.
The number of students ___ increasing.
The teacher along with the students ___ going on a trip.
Neither the manager nor his assistants ___ present.

solve.label: Book practice, 45 minutes
solve.book: WM 'Concord': all short exercises (about 40 sentences).

g.title: GA: Indian Polity I (Constitution, rights, duties)

parts.name: Part 1: Making of the Constitution and the Preamble

read.book: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity
read.where: Chapters 'Historical Background', 'Making of the Constitution', 'Salient Features', 'Preamble'

read.book: NCERT Class 11, Indian Constitution at Work
read.where: Chapter 1 'Constitution: Why and How?' (free at ncert.nic.in)

notes: Constituent Assembly: formed under the Cabinet Mission Plan 1946. First meeting 9 Dec 1946 (Sachchidananda Sinha temporary chairman). Dr Rajendra Prasad elected permanent president on 11 Dec 1946.
Objectives Resolution moved by Nehru on 13 Dec 1946, adopted 22 Jan 1947. Drafting Committee set up 29 Aug 1947, chairman Dr B. R. Ambedkar.
Constitution adopted 26 Nov 1949 (took 2 years 11 months 18 days) and came into force 26 Jan 1950. Originally 395 Articles, 22 Parts, 8 Schedules. Now 12 Schedules.
Preamble keywords: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic; Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity. 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' added by the 42nd Amendment (1976).
Berubari Union case (1960): Preamble is not part of the Constitution. Kesavananda Bharati case (1973): Preamble IS part of the Constitution.

Sources borrowed: UK: parliamentary system, rule of law. USA: Fundamental Rights, judicial review, Vice-President. Ireland: DPSP, Rajya Sabha nominations. Canada: strong Centre, residuary powers. Australia: Concurrent List, joint sitting. USSR: Fundamental Duties. Weimar Germany: emergency provisions. South Africa: amendment procedure.

examples.q: Who moved the Objectives Resolution?
Which Amendment added 'Socialist' and 'Secular' to the Preamble?
From which country did India take the Concurrent List?
Chairman of the Drafting Committee?

solve.label: Make a one-page chart
solve.book: On a sheet, write dates and names from the notes above. Cover and recite twice.

parts.name: Part 2: Fundamental Rights (Articles 12 to 35)

read.book: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity
NCERT Class 11, Indian Constitution at Work

notes: Six rights: Equality (14-18), Freedom (19-22), Exploitation (23-24), Religion (25-28), Cultural and Educational (29-30), Constitutional Remedies (32).
Art 14 equality before law. 15 no discrimination. 16 equal opportunity in public jobs. 17 abolishes untouchability. 18 abolishes titles.

Art 19: freedom of speech, assembly (peaceful, without arms), association, movement, residence, profession. Property was removed from FR by the 44th Amendment (1978); it is now Art 300A, a legal right.
Art 20: no ex post facto law, no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination. Art 21: life and personal liberty. Art 21A: education for ages 6-14 (86th Amendment, 2002). Art 22: safeguards on arrest.
Art 23: ban on forced labour and trafficking. Art 24: no child (under 14) in factories or hazardous work.
Art 32: Right to move the Supreme Court (Dr Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul'). Art 226 gives High Courts similar writ power.
Five writs: Habeas Corpus (produce the person), Mandamus (we command), Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto (by what authority).

examples.q: Which Article abolishes untouchability?
Which Article is 'Right to Constitutional Remedies'?
Which writ literally means 'to have the body'?
Property is now under which Article?

solve.label: Make a table
solve.book: Write the six rights with their Article ranges, then one Article for each (14, 17, 19, 21, 23, 25, 29, 32). Cover and recall.

parts.name: Part 3: DPSP and Fundamental Duties

read.book: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity
read.where: Chapters 'Directive Principles of State Policy' and 'Fundamental Duties'

read.book: NCERT Class 11, Indian Constitution at Work
read.where: Chapter 2 sections on DPSP and duties

notes: DPSP: Part IV, Articles 36-51. Not justiciable (cannot be enforced in court). Borrowed from Ireland.

Three groups: Socialistic, Gandhian (Art 40 village panchayats, Art 43 cottage industries, Art 47 prohibition), Liberal-intellectual (Art 44 Uniform Civil Code, Art 50 separation of judiciary from executive, Art 51 international peace).
Art 39A free legal aid, Art 43A workers in management, Art 48A environment: added by the 42nd Amendment (1976).
Art 51 (international peace and respect for treaties) is the basis of India's foreign policy: useful for MEA.

Fundamental Duties: Part IVA, Article 51A, added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on the Swaran Singh Committee. Originally 10. The 11th (parents/guardians to provide education for ages 6-14) was added by the 86th Amendment (2002).
FR vs DPSP: FR are justiciable and protect individuals; DPSP are not justiciable and guide the State.

examples.q: Which Article asks the State to promote international peace?
Which Article deals with the Uniform Civil Code?
From which country were Fundamental Duties borrowed?
How many Fundamental Duties are there now?

solve.label: Make a comparison chart
solve.book: FR vs DPSP vs FD: three columns, five lines each from the notes.

parts.name: Part 1: Profit and loss basics

read.book: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude
read.where: Chapter 'Profit and Loss': theory and solved examples

read.book: Kiran, SSC Maths Chapterwise Solved Papers
read.where: Chapter 'Profit and Loss': first 10 solved questions

notes: Profit = SP − CP. Loss = CP − SP. Profit % and Loss % are always on CP.
SP = CP × (100 + P)/100 for profit, CP × (100 − L)/100 for loss. CP = SP × 100/(100 ± %).
Fraction trick: profit 25% = 1/4, so SP : CP = 5 : 4. Profit 12.5% = 1/8, so SP : CP = 9 : 8. Loss 20% = 1/5, so SP : CP = 4 : 5.
If CP of x articles = SP of y articles, profit % = (x − y)/y × 100.
Two articles sold at the same price, one at p% gain and the other at p% loss: overall loss = p²/100 %.
Sold in a chain (A to B to C): multiply the multipliers. 20% profit then 25% profit = × 1.2 × 1.25 = × 1.5.

examples.q: CP ₹800, profit 25%. Find SP.
An article is sold for ₹1,080 at a 10% loss. Find CP.
A shopkeeper marks goods 20% above cost and gives 10% discount. Find profit %.
Two articles are sold at ₹1,000 each, one at 20% gain and one at 20% loss. Find overall result.
CP of 15 articles = SP of 12 articles. Find profit %.

solve.label: Book practice, 60 minutes max
solve.book: RSA 'Profit and Loss': first 40 questions of the first exercise.

solve.label: Previous-year questions
solve.book: KM 'Profit and Loss': 25 questions, 45 seconds each.

parts.name: Part 2: Discount and marked price

read.book: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude
read.where: Chapter 'Discount' (and the discount section of Profit & Loss)

read.book: Kiran, SSC Maths Chapterwise Solved Papers

notes: Discount is always on Marked Price (MP). SP = MP × (100 − d)/100.
Successive discounts a% and b%: single equivalent = a + b − ab/100. 20% and 10% = 28%.
To find MP when profit and discount are given: CP → SP (profit) → MP = SP × 100/(100 − d).
Discount % = (MP − SP)/MP × 100.
Trick: if a trader gives d% discount and still earns profit p%, markup % = (100 + p)/(100 − d) × 100 − 100.

examples.q: MP ₹2,500, discount 12%. Find SP.
A trader gets 20% profit after a 10% discount on MP. CP is ₹900. Find MP.
Single discount equal to successive 15% and 20%?
An article marked ₹500 is sold at ₹425. Find discount %.

parts.name: Part 3: Dishonest dealing and chains

read.book: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude
read.where: Profit and Loss: false weights and successive transaction questions

read.book: Kiran, SSC Maths Chapterwise Solved Papers

notes: False weight: gain % = (True weight − False weight)/False weight × 100 (when sold at cost).
Equation method: write CP as 100%, then everything else as % of CP. If an extra ₹x changes the result from −a% to +b%, then (a + b)% of CP = x.
Chain deals: CP of first = Final price / (multiplier 1 × multiplier 2).

examples.q: A shopkeeper uses a 900 g weight for 1 kg and sells at cost. Find gain %.
Selling at 5% loss. If SP were ₹100 more, it would be a 5% gain. Find CP.
A sells to B at 20% profit, B sells to C at 25% profit. C pays ₹1,500. Find A's CP.
SP ₹480 gives 20% loss. What SP gives 10% gain?

parts.name: Part 1: Letter coding

read.book: R.S. Aggarwal, Verbal & Non-Verbal Reasoning

parts.name: Part 1: Articles

read.book: Wren & Martin, High School English Grammar & Composition
S.P. Bakshi, Objective General English

notes: 'A' before a consonant SOUND (a university, a European, a one-rupee note). 'An' before a vowel SOUND (an hour, an honest man, an MBA).
'The' for specific or unique things: the sun, the Ganga, the Himalayas, the Gita, the Times of India, the poor, the best.
No article before proper names, languages, meals, games, subjects in general (English, lunch, cricket).
'The' with musical instruments: She plays the violin. No article with games: He plays cricket.
'A few' = some. 'Few' = hardly any. 'A little' = some. 'Little' = hardly any.

examples.q: He is ___ honest man.
examples.s: Honest starts with a vowel sound.

examples.q: ___ Ganga is a holy river.
He is ___ European.

solve.book: WM 'The Article': all short exercises.

parts.name: Part 2: Prepositions

read.book: Wren & Martin, High School English Grammar & Composition
S.P. Bakshi, Objective General English

notes: Time: at 5 pm, at night, on Monday, on 15 August, in 2020, in the morning, in March.
Place: at the station (point), in Delhi (inside), on the table (surface).
Between = two things. Among = more than two. Since = point in time. For = period of time.
Fixed pairs: good at, fond of, afraid of, accused of, suffering from, married to, interested in, congratulate on, prefer X to Y, senior to, junior to, angry with a person / at a thing.
By = agent or deadline (by 5 pm). With = instrument (cut with a knife).

examples.q: She is fond ___ music.
He was born ___ 15 August 1990.
They divided the sweets ___ the three children.
He congratulated me ___ my success.

solve.book: WM 'The Preposition': exercises (about 40 sentences).

parts.name: Part 3: Error spotting method

read.book: S.P. Bakshi, Objective General English
read.where: Chapter 'Spotting Errors': read the full method and rules

read.book: Wren & Martin, High School English Grammar & Composition
read.where: Revise concord, tense, pronoun and preposition chapters quickly

notes: Read the sentence in its four parts. Most errors are in ONE of these: subject-verb agreement, tense, preposition, article, pronoun case, adjective/adverb, word order.
Check each part in this order: verb with subject, tense clue words (yesterday, since), preposition after the verb, article before the noun.
'Less' for uncountable (less water), 'fewer' for countable (fewer people). 'Many' countable, 'much' uncountable.
'Each other' for two, 'one another' for more than two. 'Neither' for two, 'none' for more.
No double comparison: not 'more better' or 'most unkindest'.
If every part seems right, the answer is usually 'No error' (about 1 in 5 questions).

examples.q: Find the error: 'He is (a) more taller (b) than his brother (c).'
Find the error: 'Neither of the boys (a) have finished (b) their homework (c).'
Find the error: 'She has been working (a) here since (b) five years (c).'

solve.label: Book practice, 45 minutes
solve.book: SB 'Spotting Errors': 40 sentences, 40 seconds each.

g.title: GA: Indian Polity II (Union and State government)

parts.name: Part 1: President, Vice-President, PM and Council of Ministers

read.book: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity
NCERT Class 11, Indian Constitution at Work

notes: President: Article 52. Elected by an electoral college (Art 54) of elected MPs and MLAs. Minimum age 35. Term 5 years. Oath by the Chief Justice of India.
Vice-President: Article 63. Ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha (Art 64). Elected by members of both Houses (Art 66).
PM: Article 75. Appointed by the President; leader of the majority party in Lok Sabha. Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to Lok Sabha (Art 75(3)).
President can issue ordinances (Art 123) when Parliament is not in session; they must be approved within 6 weeks of reassembly.
Emergencies: Art 352 National, Art 356 President's Rule in a State, Art 360 Financial.
Pardoning power of the President: Art 72.

examples.q: Who administers the President's oath?
Which Article gives the President power to make ordinances?
To whom is the Council of Ministers collectively responsible?
Minimum age to be President?

solve.label: Make a one-page chart
solve.book: Columns: Post / Article / Elected by / Term / Minimum age / Oath by. Fill from the notes and cover and recite.

parts.name: Part 2: Parliament and the Judiciary

read.book: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity
NCERT Class 11, Indian Constitution at Work

notes: Lok Sabha: maximum 550 (530 States + 20 UTs); term 5 years; Speaker elected by its members. Rajya Sabha: maximum 250 (238 elected + 12 nominated); permanent House; one-third retire every 2 years; Vice-President is its Chairman.
Money Bill: introduced only in Lok Sabha (Art 110). Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes within 14 days.
Joint sitting (Art 108) presided over by the Speaker. Never used for a Money Bill or Constitutional amendment.
Supreme Court: Art 124; retirement age 65; original, appellate, advisory (Art 143) jurisdiction. High Courts: Art 214; retirement age 62.
Judges are removed by impeachment: a special majority in both Houses.
Public Interest Litigation (PIL): introduced by the Supreme Court; any citizen can file.

examples.q: Where can a Money Bill be introduced?
Maximum strength of Rajya Sabha?
Retirement age of Supreme Court judges?
Which Article allows the President to take the Supreme Court's advice?

solve.label: Make a chart
solve.book: Lok Sabha vs Rajya Sabha: strength, term, presiding officer, special powers.

parts.name: Part 3: State government and Panchayati Raj

read.book: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity
NCERT Class 11, Indian Constitution at Work

notes: Governor: Art 153. Appointed by the President; 5-year term; must be 35 or older. Chief Minister is appointed by the Governor and is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly (Art 164).
Governor's discretionary powers: reserving a Bill for the President (Art 200), recommending President's Rule (Art 356).
State legislature: Legislative Assembly (60 to 500 members), Legislative Council in 6 states (Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh).

Panchayati Raj: 73rd Amendment 1992, in force 1993, Part IX, Articles 243 to 243O, 11th Schedule. Three tiers: Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti, Zila Parishad. 5-year term; reservation for women (one-third).
Municipalities: 74th Amendment, Part IXA, 12th Schedule.
Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended a three-tier Panchayati Raj.

examples.q: Which Amendment gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj?
Which Article deals with President's Rule in a State?
Which Schedule lists Panchayat subjects?
Who appoints the Chief Minister?

solve.label: Make a chart
solve.book: 73rd vs 74th Amendment: part, articles, schedule, bodies.

parts.name: Part 1: Simple interest

read.book: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude
read.where: Chapter 'Simple Interest': theory and solved examples

read.book: Kiran, SSC Maths Chapterwise Solved Papers

notes: SI = P × R × T / 100. Amount A = P + SI = P(1 + RT/100). T is in years; convert months (9 months = 0.75).
A sum becomes double at SI in 100/R years, triple in 200/R years.
If the same sum is lent to two persons at different rates, add the separate interests: SI total = P × (R1 T1 + R2 T2)/100.
Banker's tip: for 1 year, 10% of P is P/10; for 2 years at 5%, it is also P/10.

examples.q: Find the simple interest on ₹6,000 at 8% for 3 years.
At what rate does ₹5,000 become ₹6,200 in 4 years (SI)?
In how many years does a sum double at 12.5% SI?

parts.name: Part 2: Compound interest

read.book: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude
Kiran, SSC Maths Chapterwise Solved Papers

notes: Amount A = P (1 + R/100)^T. CI = A − P.
Half-yearly: rate R/2, time 2T. Quarterly: rate R/4, time 4T.
CI − SI for 2 years = P (R/100)². For 3 years = P (R/100)² (3 + R/100).
Memorise the multipliers: 10% two years = 1.21; 20% two years = 1.44; 5% two years = 1.1025; 10% three years = 1.331.

examples.q: Find CI on ₹10,000 at 10% for 2 years.
Difference between CI and SI on ₹8,000 at 5% for 2 years?

r.title: Reasoning: Blood relations and direction sense

parts.name: Part 1: Blood relations (basic)

read.book: R.S. Aggarwal, Verbal & Non-Verbal Reasoning
read.where: Chapter 'Blood Relations': theory and first exercise

read.book: Kiran, SSC Reasoning Chapterwise Solved Papers

notes: Draw a family tree. Use □ for male, ○ for female, = for married, vertical lines for children.
Mother's brother = maternal uncle. Father's brother = paternal uncle (chacha/tau). Mother's sister = maternal aunt (mausi). Father's sister = paternal aunt (bua).
Father's father = paternal grandfather. Mother's father = maternal grandfather. Brother's wife = sister-in-law. Wife's brother = brother-in-law.
Son of mother's brother or sister = cousin. Wife's mother = mother-in-law.
When a sentence says 'my father's only son', that is the speaker himself (if male).

examples.q: A is B's sister. C is B's mother. D is C's father. E is D's mother. How is A related to D?
examples.s: C is A's mother; D is C's father, so D is A's grandfather.

examples.q: Pointing to a lady, a man says, 'Her son is my son's maternal uncle.' How is the lady related to the man?
examples.s: Her son is the brother of the man's wife, so she is the wife's mother.

examples.q: A is brother of B, B is sister of C, C is father of D. How is A related to D?
examples.s: A is C's brother, so D's uncle.

solve.label: Book practice, 40 minutes
solve.book: RV 'Blood Relations': 30 questions, drawing a tree for each.

solve.label: Previous-year questions
solve.book: KR: 20 questions.

parts.name: Part 2: Blood relations (coded)

read.book: R.S. Aggarwal, Verbal & Non-Verbal Reasoning
Kiran, SSC Reasoning Chapterwise Solved Papers

notes: In coded relations, write each symbol's meaning at the top and rewrite the statement as a chain.
Example code: A + B = A is mother of B; A − B = A is brother of B; A × B = A is father of B.
Convert to a family tree before answering, never guess from the symbols.

examples.q: A + B means A is mother of B; A − B means A is brother of B; A × B means A is father of B. What does P × Q − R mean?
examples.s: P is father of Q; Q is brother of R, so P is also R's father.

examples.q: With the same code, what does P + Q × R mean?
examples.s: P is mother of Q; Q is father of R.

parts.name: Part 3: Direction sense

read.book: R.S. Aggarwal, Verbal & Non-Verbal Reasoning
Kiran, SSC Reasoning Chapterwise Solved Papers

notes: Draw a map from the starting point. Take north as up. A right turn from north is east; from east is south.
Shortest distance = √(a² + b²) for perpendicular legs. Learn triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17.
In the morning the shadow falls to the west; in the evening to the east (the Sun is in the east in the morning).
Left turn rotates 90° anticlockwise. Facing north and turning right then left then left ends facing west.

examples.q: A man walks 5 km north and then 12 km east. How far is he from the start?
Facing north, you turn right, then left, then left. Which way do you face?
Rahul goes 10 m south, turns left and walks 20 m, then turns left and walks 10 m. Where is he from the start?
examples.s: South 10, east 20, north 10 brings him level with the start, 20 m east.

parts.name: Part 1: Company rule to the Revolt of 1857

read.book: Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India
read.where: Chapters on 'Advent of Europeans', 'Expansion of British Power', 'Revolt of 1857'

read.book: NCERT Class 8, Our Pasts III (History)
read.where: Chapters 1 to 6, quick read (free at ncert.nic.in)

notes: Battle of Plassey 23 June 1757: Robert Clive beat Siraj-ud-Daulah. Battle of Buxar 22 Oct 1764: Hector Munro beat Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah and Shah Alam II. Treaty of Allahabad 1765: Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the Company.
Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley): Hyderabad first (1798). Doctrine of Lapse (Dalhousie): Satara first (1848), then Jhansi, Nagpur.
Land revenue: Permanent Settlement 1793 (Cornwallis, zamindars). Ryotwari (Thomas Munro, Madras). Mahalwari (Holt Mackenzie, 1822, North-West).

Revolt of 1857: started at Meerut on 10 May 1857. Leaders: Bahadur Shah Zafar (Delhi), Nana Sahib (Kanpur), Rani Lakshmibai (Jhansi), Begum Hazrat Mahal (Lucknow), Kunwar Singh (Bihar). Lord Canning was Governor-General.
After 1857: Government of India Act 1858 ended Company rule. Queen's Proclamation 1 Nov 1858. Canning became the first Viceroy.

examples.q: Where did the Revolt of 1857 begin?
Who started the Subsidiary Alliance?
Which Act ended Company rule?
Who was the first Viceroy?

solve.label: Make a timeline
solve.book: Write 1757, 1764, 1765, 1793, 1798, 1848, 1857, 1858 with one line each. Recite twice.

read.book: Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India
read.where: Chapters 'Socio-Religious Reform Movements' and 'Early Nationalists / Moderates and Extremists'

read.book: NCERT Class 8, Our Pasts III

notes: Brahmo Samaj 1828 (Raja Ram Mohan Roy; sati banned 1829 under Bentinck). Arya Samaj 1875 (Dayanand Saraswati). Ramakrishna Mission 1897 (Vivekananda). Satyashodhak Samaj 1873 (Jyotiba Phule). Prarthana Samaj 1867 (Atmaram Pandurang). Aligarh movement: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan, MAO College 1875.
INC founded Dec 1885 in Bombay; A. O. Hume; first president W. C. Bonnerjee. Moderates: Dadabhai Naoroji, Gokhale. Extremists: Lal-Bal-Pal.

Partition of Bengal Oct 1905 (Curzon) led to Swadeshi. Muslim League founded 1906 at Dhaka. Surat split 1907. Morley-Minto Reforms 1909 introduced separate electorates. Delhi Durbar 1911: capital moved from Calcutta to Delhi.

examples.q: Who founded the Brahmo Samaj?
Who founded the Arya Samaj?
Who was the first Congress president?

parts.name: Part 3: The Gandhian era to Independence

read.book: Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India

read.book: NCERT Class 12, Themes in Indian History III

notes: Gandhi returned 1915. Champaran 1917, Ahmedabad mill strike 1918, Kheda 1918. Rowlatt Act 1919. Jallianwala Bagh 13 Apr 1919.

Non-Cooperation 1920-22 (withdrawn after Chauri Chaura 1922). Simon Commission 1928. Purna Swaraj resolution Lahore Dec 1929. Dandi March 12 Mar 1930. Gandhi-Irwin Pact 1931. Poona Pact 1932 (Gandhi and Ambedkar). Government of India Act 1935.

Cripps Mission 1942. Quit India 8 Aug 1942 ('Do or Die'). INA led by Subhas Chandra Bose from 1943. Cabinet Mission 1946. Mountbatten Plan 3 June 1947. Indian Independence Act July 1947. Independence 15 Aug 1947.

examples.q: In which year was the Dandi March?
Which pact settled seats for the Depressed Classes?
Which mission came in 1946?
When was the Quit India Movement launched?
